In 1765, the Ashaini economy is the 16th largest in the world by nominal GDP and the 20th largest by PPP GDP. It is a large, industrialized, privatized, technologically developing economy. It is best characterized through its implementation of the ideas of the Imperial New School wherein the government acts primarily as a moderator for the private market in defense of the consumer. The economy is heavily centered around the production of industrial goods, with primary economic sectors being the shipbuilding, oil refining, and steel manufacturing sectors. The economy is projected to benefit from high growth rates over the following years due to a high birth rate and quickly increasing per worker productivity. The national currency is the Ashaini Mejit.  

The national historically relied on heavy centralized planning to guide the economy, though has in the post-war environment employed a heavily regulated free-market model. In recent history, the economy been marred by high inflation rates despite little quantitative easing, and KDTI metrics remain low proportionate to GDP/C. 
=== Historical Economic Structure ===
The economic structure of Ashain has historically been one of top down control of economic forces, either through ownership or through legal directives. Throughout most of Ashain’s history, the economy has been controlled directly by the [[Imperial family of Ashain|imperial family]] in control of the [[Ashaini Imperial Throne|Camphour Throne]]. In the [[Mishizhiki era]], the economy, while still nominally being the personal property of the emperor, was de-facto controlled by the state through a large number of government agencies and government owned companies. In the post-war era, the Ashaini economy continued this state owned, top down model until the passing of the Minue Bill, marking the economy’s transition into its modern privatized state. Funding for social programs and non-industrial economic programs were chronically underfunded, typically under the justification of a need to enter a competitive war footing as quickly as possible. While the focus on policy has produced results such as the [[National Defense Economy]], standards of living have been poor throughout its industrialized history as a result. 
==== Pre-Mishizhiki Economy ====
Before industrialization, the economy consisted of a rural population split between subsistence farmers outside irrigation networks and those farming in centralized irrigated rice paddy systems and an urban population in cities and towns. The economy was fundamentally agrarian and centralized, with ownership of the entire nation vested in the Imperial Throne. The crown would delegate overseers to its directly controlled lands in what is the modern-day [[Sjoran Metropolitan Zone|Sjoran metropolis]] and grant provincial lords dominion over more distant provinces, who in turn would centralize their own farming. The country would initially utilize a standardized barter system in areas directly controlled by lords or the crown, though this would transition over time to the use of coin from the [[Imperial Mint]]. Most coinage was copper, silver, or gold, with certain bronze coinages circulating as exceptions. It would produce and regulate the [[Kobu]], a rectangular coin with a similarly shaped hole punched in the middle. The nobility would also frequently pay workers in rice, leather, salt, and wood rather than in coin for manual labor on large projects, though coin was often used for intercity trade, payment within the nobility, and payment for finished crafts. 

Farmers in frontier and more isolated areas typically escaped this scheme and instead relied on subsistence farming. These farmers were often targeted by bandits and the occasional tax collector for their harvests until the [[1157 Goodyear Campaign]], in which the state made a concerted effort to kill off roving bandit gangs and pirates, making the countryside and coastal seas more amenable to intercity trade. Soon after, these farmers would regularly interact with tax collectors of the local lords or the crown to pay for the state's continued presence in the countryside. 

Farmers in regions directly controlled by the nobility would often work both on their own farms and on those owned by the nobility. They typically lived in their own housing near the farm and would receive standard payment in rice, firewood, or coin. Outside the harvesting season, they would also frequently be mobilized for public projects such as dams, irrigation, walls, and storage buildings. Farmers organized themselves over time and formed towns around these irrigation networks, though this was not always the case and was uncommon in more rugged terrain. 

Most of the country employed a [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regressive_tax regressive tax scheme] in which citizens of a city would be taxed by land ownership and on an excise tax on items that entered and exited the city. This tax was heavily supplemented by frequent imperial monopolies on the production of raw resources such as salt and iron. The Imperial Mint was the primary source of income for the state as it controlled both tax collection schemes and the issuing of new mint.

==== Mishizhiki Era Industry ====
The national economy immediately following the [[Mishizhiki Revival]] until the [[Treaty of Freedom]] was largely characterized by aggressive growth of heavy and arms industries driven through national ownership and investment, typically at the cost of other production and profit maximizing. The large majority of the nation’s GDP was produced through state owned industries and state directed companies. While technically no independent companies existed as all companies existed under lease, there were practically independent companies which found success. Outside of sheer productive capacity, the day to day living conditions of the country remained largely impoverished. Significant portions of domestic consumer goods production came out of the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Putting-out_system#Cottage_industry cottage industry] which, due to a lack of economies of scale, frequently resulted in insufficient quantities of goods to suppress inflationary prices as household incomes grew through industrialization. The internal market regularly lacked strong food security, a plenty of consumer goods, civilian access to fuel, and certain chemical goods related to the production of critical war goods. 

In the pre-war period, significant efforts were spent towards producing a more [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autarky autarkic] economy. The greatest state energies were directed towards the independent production of foodstuffs to resist embargo. The production of agricultural goods was mainly controlled by [[Ashaini Heavy Industries]] and the [[Mountainhand Station]] conglomerates. The vast majority of state lead agricultural efforts were concentrated towards the production of rice and basic foodstuffs, as it was deemed too land inefficient to have significant feed production slated for meat production. Instead, the state promoted fisheries, both for the vast aquacultural potential of the long coastline and the additional organic demand that would drive towards the shipbuilding industry. Additionally, the oil sector became a significant player in the country’s economy for the first time. Oil exports made up for a substantial portion of accrued foreign currency, and granted the country a degree of energy independence. This energy independence was exploited to provide cheap energy to energy intensive domestic heavy industry like aluminum production.  

The fiscal situation of the country was constantly under stress, and was practically always under the threat of defaulting to internal debt holders. Defaulting on international debts was never seriously considered due to the fear of withdrawal of international investment and possible military intervention. Despite this, Ashaini [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_rating credit rating] was historically poor. Private businesses underwent forced bond buying and all banking activities were controlled by the Imperial Bank. Occasionally, significant quantitative easing measures were implemented under exceptional times, leading to a peak acute inflation rate of 27% in 1671. Despite this, the government was entirely reliant on economic growth outpacing the rate of debt growth.  

The wartime economy was marred with extreme goods shortages in the civilian sector. Practically all production was focused on the war effort, and the consumer goods pool of the country shrank in the meantime due to scrap drives. In 1693, the peak year of Ashaini war goods production, 99.3% of all aluminum production, 93.1% of all steel production, 83.9% of all crude oil production and refinement, 99.7% of all rubber and synthetic rubber production, 42.6% of timber production, 95.7% of all copper production, and 94.4% of all machined goods production were driven towards military production. 79% of the 1693 state budget was allotted for military expenditure, accounting for a deficit of 89% of then year GDP. In the last two years of the Red War, the GDP shrunk by 7% and 54% in 1764 and 1765 respectively, primarily due to ASOFCOM landings, seizures of territory, and strategic bombardment. 
==== Post War Status & Pre Minue Bill Structure ====
In the immediate post-war, the Ashaini economy was largely nonexistent. Bombardment of the cities was extensive, with an estimated 20-25% of all buildings in the country being destroyed. Many cities were either total or partially destroyed, and most rail networks were rendered inoperable. Production of goods in the days before surrender was reduced to half of pre-war levels. [[Ashain Occupation Forces Command|ASOFCOM]], through the [[Billinger Mandate]] given by the [[Allied States Dewier Decree]], set out to move all industry that remained back to respective homelands when possible, and to destroy industry when impossible. By 1697, Ashain was reduced to an entirely unmechanized agricultural state, and no meaningful industry remained in the entire length of the country. Additionally, large swathes of the remaining harvest was seized, and masses of forced labor were imported back to home countries. Combined with the state of Ashaini agriculture, this caused the [[Cold Famine]], lasting nominally from 1695 to 1710, though effects of the famine lasted until rationing was lifted fully in 1731. Not all laborers were repatriated until 1739, with the [[Ashoa 500]] being returned by XXXX.  

The country remained in a state of deindustrialization until 1706, with the allowance of the construction of several fertilizer and agricultural machinery plants in [[Sjoran]] by ASOFCOM in response to the ongoing famine. The first industries outside of the purview of ASOFCOM was created under the [[1707 Internal Security Bill]], which sought to bring back a level of industrialization to grant the state an ability to wage a limited guerrilla campaign if ASOFCOM forces were to clamp down on state activities. Most of this industrialization was rolled back by 1711 with the uncovering of this scheme and the destruction of the limited industries set up under this scheme with the [[Red Circle Incident]]. From the end of the war to the mid 1710’s, practically all state activities were focused on increasing agricultural output to suppress famine. No additional industry was built until the [[1716 National Defense Reconstruction Act]]. 

Serious industrial reconstruction efforts began in 1716, with the passing of the National Defense Reconstruction Act and the [[National Reconstruction Bill]]. Additionally, the [[Pereces Funding Schema]] was implemented in 1717 under the [[Akazashi cabinet]] to fund current and future reconstruction. Civilian labor was mobilized for large infrastructure projects like the [[Taiho Dam]] or the [[Sjoran Metropole Network]] (later known as the Capital Metropole Network), and heavy taxation was implemented on the populace. In the same year, over three dozen bureaus were established, most notable being the [[Bureau of Heavy Industry]], the [[Defense Industries Bureau]], the [[Bureau of Light Industries]], the [[Bureau of Resources]], and the [[Bureau of Technology]]. Additionally, several bureaus such as the [[Bureau of Transportation]] and [[Bureau of Education]] were expanded beyond their previous skeleton staffs. From the establishment of this bureaus until the [[Minue Bill]], much of the economy was centered around state-led industrialization efforts unified around the ideas of the [[Minue Doctrine]] first crystallized under the [[1715 Sjora Institute Government Whitepaper]]. The government would first have a whole-of-society mobilization of resources to industrialize as quickly as possible in order to avert a second destruction of the national economy through foreign invasion, and after a point of sufficient deterrence had been achieved, the private market would take over to stimulate national economic growth at internationally competitive rates. The Ashaini economy, mostly through secret Dahean aid, grew rapidly. By 1739, Ashain had achieved pre-war levels of heavy industrial output, though the economy was still overall smaller. The economy was moved away from the majority state run strategy by 1744 with the passing of the Minue Bill. 
=== Modern Economic Structure ===
Much of the modern day domestic economy is largely shaped through the passing of the Minue Bill in 1744, marking the large scale privatization of the economy, the mass expansion of the private market, and the dejure mass dissolution of bureaus and their transformation into legally separate entities. Most fiscal expenditures of the government is spent towards military and regulatory expenditures, with an emphasis placed on reducing taxes as extensively as possible. The Ashaini bond is regarded as one of the safest bonds in the world due to low debt to GDP, low interest payments, and a general government reluctance to sell bonds to the foreign market. 

The Ashaini economy and state expenditure is generally suited towards industrial output and industrial capacity growth. As a result, many KDTI drivers like passenger rail, small canal networks, rural road networks, and energy efficacy infrastructure are presently undeveloped.  
<!-- Not sure if it's really reasonable to say that, of all things, city transport infrastructure is undeveloped in a used-to-be centralized state. It has one of the best RoIs in a very obvious capacity so idk, probably change. --> 

The Ashaini government expressly attempts to run small deficits and minimize their tax rates in lower tax brackets as an attempt to maximize economic growth, though this has repeatedly led to fiscal crises and political turmoil born from such crises. The government often needs to leverage emergency revenue streams to pay for yearly obligatory budgetary items like subsidies and military expenditure, and the non-healthcare social expenditure per capita of the country is the lowest in the world amongst developed nations. 
==== Ashani Small Government ====
The present day state of the Ashani government and it's policy towards the private market, as written in the Declaration of Reason section of the [[1717 Market-Government Relationship Bill]], primarily revolves around the growth of total real purchasing power within the economy through an incentive-based structure of market laws. Put simply, the state is to maintain low taxes to keep as much capital as possible within the free market, and rather than directly controlling entities and assets, will instead structure the market legal code to provide incentives for growth in value or velocity intense sectors of the economy. Such a model has caused the size of the government to be smaller than the international average, with public sector employment being only 3.9 percent of total employment.<ref>Add number about government employment here or something go cite a government website.</ref> It primarily focuses on the regulation of market forces and the guarantee of fair practices against the consumer.

The current model has drawn considerable criticism from contemporary economists.<ref>Cite some open letter by a bunch of domestic and some foreign economists which say that this should have only been a transitionary model of economic growth.</ref> Primary concerns include the ability of the government to provide important state functions, such as its weak pension program, a lack of universal healthcare, a lack of free college, a weak unemployment benefits system, and a lax attitude towards immigration control; the inability of the government to draw taxes so it may sustain its subsidies and defense spending; the rare use of bonds in the domestic market, which deprives the citizenry of an ultra-safe money parking method; concerns over the government's overreliance on regulatory agencies, which may regulate growth and allow businesses to lead policy rather than the state; and the high velocity nature of the market typically outstripping growth of goods production, forcing high interest rates and a bar on quantitative easing to regulate inflation.
==== Government Involvement in the Economy ====
A large portion of government involvement within the economy involves the regulation of actions by private entities with the stated goal of maximizing competitiveness and incentivizing capex to be a large portion of entity expenditure as to maximize the production of goods and value-adding jobs.<ref>Reference the page of the bill</ref> Such regulation is mainly headed by the [[Securities and Consumer Exchange Directorate]] (SCED), which regulates securities exchanges and consumer protection in the financial sector; the [[Bureau of Environmental Hazards]] (BEH), which works to minimize environmental pollution, monitors and minimizes the dangers of certain environmental features such as hurricanes or volcanoes, and enforces standards on food, water, soil, and air quality; the [[Labour Standards Commission]] (LSC), which sets and enforces labour safety standards and safeguard employees' rights to unionization and unfair or unsafe work conditions; and the [[Anti-Trust Commission]] (ATC), which regulates mergers, enforces antitrust and consumer protection laws. 

Article 4 of the Minue Bill acts as the foundation of modern Ashaini regulatory law. It formally consecrates and defines the state’s ability to regulate mergers, dissolve monopolies, enforce expenditure controls on companies, suppress anti consumer actions, and back private market action.  The 2nd Amendment on Private Market Activity which followed the Minue Bill in 1747 regulates the maximum profit margin that a company at certain size brackets can accrue to be spent towards non-capex and non-business emergency fund spending. Article 4 and the 2nd Amendment remain controversial amongst both business and consumer populations, with dissatisfaction to the government powers peaking early in its lifetime with the dissolution of the Tenpeaks company in 1751. More recent high profile actions include the denial of the Minsokoa-Hadrian merger, the arrest of the Atlas Cabal and the general existence of the cabal altogether, and the currently ongoing Armalite v Regency case and the denial of Armalite’s purchase of Uldan Inc. 
==== Government Fiscal Policy ====
Despite the small government budget, much of it is reserved for direct subsidies of industries considered critical to the economic or military security of the nation.<ref>Refer to some government justification report on why so much money was being spent on subsidies like a GAO report.</ref> <s>Out of the 18,968,564,335,000 Mejit FY 1765 government budget, I'll probably redo this section later idk I just need a better grasp on subsidization</s> These sectors receive further support through generous loans from state banks, funding research and development of related fields, tax exemptions, subsidized energy inputs, providing bonds as a government-backed security, and tariffs. Some sectors include the shipbuilding, chemical manufacturing, electronics manufacturing, and steel manufacturing industries.
Due to the high velocity nature of the economy, the government struggles to maintain a healthy rate of inflation. The state typically employs high interest rates on government loans to filter for the creation and growth of safe, high return businesses and reduce inflation<ref>throw in a citation from the fed equivalent.</ref>. Quantitative easing, however, has an upper cap as set by the yester-year inflation rate when the economy is not in a recession, as set by the [[1721 Debt Control Bill]] to slow the growth of the total capital pool within the economy. 

The Ashaini government's ability to sell bonds is also set to a YTD cap by the [[1721 Debt Control Bill]]. Public debt to the domestic bond market can only reach 35 of GDP in times of non recession or non crisis, and currently sits at 34.4% debt-to-GDP<ref>Yet again throw in a governnment source.</ref>. Due to the extreme limiting of the selling of bonds, yields tend to be below inflation rates, and as a result borrowing costs are consequently low<ref>Cite some bond yield rate thing from the government.</ref>. The foreign bond market is similarly limited to an even smaller 10% of GDP, though foreign bonds are more used as a means to disseminate the currency amongst poorer nations so they may buy goods from Ashain<ref>Cite a leak from some internal wolfowitz-esc document.</ref>. 

The treasury frequently struggles to maintain budgetary stability and upkeep even currently existing expenditures. Income tax rates amongst lower and middle brackets remain low despite opposition from politicians within the ruling coalition. Additionally, company tax rates similarly remain low to stimulate industrial growth. This has strained the government’s ability to collect revenue sufficient to grow its expenditure to a size expected for the size of its population. The debt ceiling has been raised twice, first in 1753 from 20% to 30% of GDP, and again in 1761 from 30% to 35% of GDP. The 1760 activation of the Mint’s currency production beyond the 1731 Kiwaza Fiscal Control Act for the sake of quantitative easing under the auspices of the [[Mahen Financial Crisis of 1759]] remains today, drawing significant criticism from political fiscal hawks and internal watch agencies. The activation contributed to the peaking of inflation since 1727 at 7.1% YoY inflation in 1762. Much of the state revenue comes from taxation on oil profits and the profits of the State Investiture Authority, with both consisting 37% of annual state revenue. Tariffs also make up a considerable portion of state revenue. Tariffs are generally targeted at imported complex products like industrial machinery, computation hardware, and mining equipment, though large tariffs do also exist for things like agricultural and textile products for specific staple goods. Tariffs make up 9% of state revenue. 
=== Ashain in the Global Economy ===
Ashain primarily exports crude oil, refined oil, ships, and steel to the global market, being one of the largest producers of ships and refined oil in the world. Additionally, Ashain has a small international banking sector, often attracting mid sized institutions through relatively low sector tax rates.

====== Arms Exports ======
Due to its relatively limited size and technological unsophistication of the domestic defense sector, the Ashaini defense market plays a minor role in the foreign export market, exporting primarily missiles such as the TR-200 BVRAAM and JSDW, with the only break from this pattern being the export of its Type-30 light tank.

====== Oil Extraction ======
The Ashaini economy extracted 1,744,000 barrels of oil in 1765, the 14th largest extractor of oil in the world. Extraction represents a significant fraction of the economy, being X% of 1765 GDP. The country mostly produces light, sweet oil, with both the X and X oilfields, the nation’s largest oilfields, being of that type of oil. So far, no heavier or more sour oil fields have been tapped. 

The Ashaini government has made significant investments into the sector for the purposes of economic growth, revenue growth, and national security. The sector has historically been and remains a very large recipient of subsidies, once peaking at  43% of all subsidy expenditure in 1649. Currently, the sector is the second largest recipient of subsidies, and, with the oil refining industry, is the only sector to receive negative interest loans. The oil extraction business is mandated to provide extensive physical and cybersecurity measures to all oil rigs, and all oil rigs must be able to go underway under their own power. Additionally, the National Energy Security Act includes a clause which allows for the nationalization/seizure of assets of the oil extraction sector in wartime. 

In recent years, concerns from internal budgetary monitors have been raised about the sustainability of the state budget in its current form as Ashaini oil fields run out. At a table extraction rate, the country’s known fields will dry out in 10 years. While current estimates range the combined proven and estimated fields to last for another 20-30 years, it is unknown whether Ashaini oil efforts can last in the long term. Various watchdogs have proposed measures to resolve this issue, such as swapping the nation’s automotive fleet to run off of electricity, reducing oil extraction rates, and reinvigorating the country’s synthetic oil sector. As of 1765, the combined oil extraction and refining sector taxation revenue makes up 30% of state revenue. The sector contributes significantly to the State Investiture Authority’s annual investment pool, with taxation revenue from the oil sector having been used to fund an average of 70% of its growth per year since its inception by the Mikan Reform Bill of 1751.

==== Oil Refining ====
The Ashaini oil refining sector, being formalized through [[Empress Miakya’s XXVIII Decree]] in 1612, is the second oldest formalized business sector and the oldest industry in the nation, being only younger than the state owned mint. At the time, however, only a minuscule amount of oil was produced from a single well, being used entirely for heating and lighting. It is only until the [[1639 Ashaini Vitalization Decree]] by Emperor Mishizhiki did the sector expand beyond this point, with the first additional wells and the first refinery finishing construction by 1646 after significant issues acquiring the requisite funding and expertise was overcome. After the Treaty of Freedom, all Ashaini oil extraction and refining were destroyed. No oil was produced until 1710, when the Bureau of Heavy Industry began to reactivate wells and build new refineries. Both refineries and wells were semi privatized with the dissolution of the Bureau of Heavy Industry, with the government retaining a 30% stake in all refinery ownership until the stake was sold off in 1759 under the Walderson Deal with the expansion of oil sector taxes.  

As of 1765, Ashain has a total refining capacity of 2,100,000 million barrels, with a 94% total capacity usage of 1,970,000 barrels a day produced in 1764. Most government constructed refineries focused on middle distillate production, so as a result roughly 2/3rds of present day Ashaini refining output produces middle distillates, primarily focusing on automotive and aviation fuels. Despite government efforts to increase refining output to suit the export market, refinery capacity and capacity growth remains concentrated in expanded former government facilities.  

The refining sector comprises roughly 1.6% of GDP in 1765, the second highest industrial contributor to GDP. Various economists (have a comical number of links here) and economic think tanks, along with internal reviews, have raised concerns about the possibility of currency appreciation caused by oil exports to make other industrial exports less competitive in the global market, and allow for domestic goods to be outcompeted by foreign ones by price.  

The sector has among the highest business income tax rates in the economy. As a result, and combined with the generally high revenue of the sector, the tax revenues from the sector comprises 16% of total state revenue. The Ashaini government frequently levies complete tax exemptions for the sector on any overhead cost related taxes, and is the only sector other than the oil extraction sector to receive negative interest loans. The National Business Ministry has been frequently criticized with excessively siding with oil companies, and has been accused by labor unions of aiding in suppressing wages. Additionally, the oil industry, being both the extraction and refining subsectors, are the only two sectors to have had both politicians and companies prosecuted over corruption charges. 
==== Defense Production ====
Ashain, with most investment coming from recent decades, has a decently sized but young defense industry which fulfills a large portion of Ashaini military goods demand. The defense sector, one of the more technologically advanced sectors, represents 0.6% of 1765 GDP being the 8th largest industrial sector in the economy despite its relatively low total employment. 

After the dismantling of all military industry through the Treaty of Freedom, no dedicated military industry existed in the country until 1707 with the passing of the Internal Security Bill, which funded various new defense programs so that a secret defense sector could be constructed to conduct an asymmetric guerrilla war if ASOFCOM forces were to attempt a dissolution of the standing government. The scheme collapsed and the existing industry was completely destroyed in 1711 with the Red Circle Incident and the events therein. With the obviation of the ISB, no new funding was allocated to defense until 1716, with the passing of the National Defense Reconstruction Act, which formalized the organization and funding of the modern form of the [[Ashaini military]] and began the reconstruction of the defense sector. Production was largely handled by the Defense Industries Bureau, with the existence of a handful of small private contractors for camouflage, until the bureau was dissolved and privatized in 1747.  

The [[Ashaini Military Industry|Ashaini military industry]] is one of the largest recipient of state subsidies(note about how it’s calculated), second only to the Ashaini shipbuilding sector. Much of the defense sector is concentrated in [[Sjoran Maritime Superindustrial Zone]] and work in close conjunction with shipbuilders due to various beneficial tax laws specific to the defense industries for the metropolitan area. Despite this, much of the wheeled vehicular production of the sector is located in [[Mikuro]] for its deeper history with domestic automotive production. The sector is the only one required to produce 12 month audits for the government and the public after the passing of the [[New Reform Bill]] in 1760.  

The sector primarily fulfills logistically oriented orders, such as military trucks, armored cars, tankers, and transport planes, as the government does not yet see the sector as capable of multiple simultaneous ongoing large defense projects(White paper here). While large projects are historically rare, some, such as the [[AZ-121 Fighter-Bomber|AZ-121 fighter-bomber]] and the failed [[Strategic Defense Airborne Command Center]] project, have existed. 
==== Machine Tools Production ====
The Ashaini machinery in the year 1765 sector produced (Lahn symbol)X dollars worth of machinery goods, representing X% of the manufacturing sector total output value adjusted or X% of GDP. Primarily focusing on heavy industrial machinery, most sector output is consumed domestically by the growing industrial sector of Ashain, with 83% of production being sold to the domestic market.  

Forming in 1642 with the Ashaini Vitalization Decree’s second amendment, the sector was formalized by the creation of the Industrial Tools Department of the Directorate of Industry. Ashain has historically struggled with domestically satisfying its industrial machinery needs, with only 44% of Ashaini industrial needs fulfilled by domestic production in 1686. In the immediate post war, nearly all domestic machinery production was destroyed by a mixture of wartime bombing and demolition by ASOFCOM, with only a single small government controlled maintenance facility in Sjoran undestroyed for the remnant mechanized farming left. Machinery production was rebooted in 1709 by the Bureau of Heavy Industry, and by 1734 had surpassed pre-war levels. After the dissolution of the bureau and the privatization of the bureau’s assets, a large portion of sector capability was concentrated in the [[Ayazami-Tatayamo Conglomerate|Ayazami-Tatayamo industrial conglomerate]], with 56% of production output concentrated in the company. Today, despite the share shrinking to 47%, government and public concerns remain over existing practices which could lead to a monopoly in the sector.  

Due to much of the sector orbiting around the activities of Ayazami-Tatayamo, much of the industry is located in [[Kaitriss]], where the company is headquartered. However, [[Grunai]], [[Zabri]], [[Tirune]], and Sjoran also host larger machinery facilities as well. A significant portion of the sector is spread out across the country for the servicing of local smaller businesses.  

After the privatization of Bureau assets, relations between industry leaders and the government became heavily strained. In 1749, the [[Ryoshin Commission]] was launched to investigate corruption ties between the government and earlier privatization efforts. The machinery industry, along with the oil industry, were the only two industries to have charges brought to them, though only the oil industry was prosecuted after the [[1750 Churchtower Assassinations]] as the commission head for the investigation of the machinery industry was killed alongside the prime minister. I’m response, though, much of the formerly existing cost subsidies were cut under the justification that domestic demand was high enough to consume all supply without the need to suppress prices. 
==== Steel Production ====
The Ashaini steel sector is the 7th largest producer of steel in the world, producing approximately 87,100,000 metric tons of steel in 1765. The sector is the largest industrial employer in the nation, and the third largest industrial sector contributor to GDP, comprising 1.5% of GDP in 1765.  

Prior to the Treaty of Freedom, Ashain was the 11th largest producer of steel in the world, producing 6,100,000 metric tons of steel in the year X. However, after the mandates required by the Treaty of Freedom, Ashaini steel production was reduced to 0-300 tons of steel annually by 1697. No new steel foundries were founded until 1702 under the remaining members of Akinro Steel. The foundry remained the only steel foundry in Ashain until 1708 when, with the formation of the Bureau of Heavy Industry, public investment into the steel sector began. By the time the bureau was dissolved in 1744, steel production had increased to 39,300,000 metric tons of steel per annum. Today, the sector averages 4.6 percent growth in capacity per year over the past 10 years, and is a major focus of Ashaini state industrial policy alongside oil and shipbuilding.  

The primary domestic buyers of steel are the shipbuilding industry, the machinery industry, and the metal goods industry, with a significant portion of production sold abroad. Due to the largest buyer being the shipbuilding sector, the steel manufacturing sector has consequently concentrated in the Sjoran metropole. The sector is yet to break heavily into the export market, with over 85% of orders coming from the domestic market.  

The Ashaini government levies high import taxes on foreign steel imports to combat cheaper foreign steel crowding out domestic production. The sector is also the recipient of low interest loans under the Goodfellow Industrial Scheme introduced in 1751, though is not the recipient of cost covering or direct subsidies unlike many other large industrial sectors.
